verdict.reasoning: Doctor concludes, “your symptoms are suggestive of something called gastroenteritis… a basic infection of your tummy,” and the patient describes “diarrhea… super watery… just pouring straight from my bum,” consistent with acute gastroenteritis with watery diarrhea.
Patient says, “I think it was… Monday, Tuesday… it’s been about three days now,” matching onset about three days ago between Monday and Tuesday.

Patient reports, “I go to the toilet and it’s just super watery… it’s just pouring straight from my bum,” and “I feel like it’s like almost every hour I’m awake,” and denies blood: “No… there’s nothing like that,” consistent with profuse watery non‑bloody diarrhea occurring about hourly.

Patient notes crampy pain: “I feel a cramp and then I know it’s time to go,” localised “at the bottom… feels pretty like in the middle to me,” and that it “comes and goes,” consistent with intermittent crampy central lower abdominal pain.

Patient states, “I definitely feel kind of nauseous… I have vomited… whenever I have like milk… I just feel like I want to vomit… one time I just… had some milk and I just completely vomited it,” matching nausea and vomiting especially with milk intake.

In response to fever query, patient says, “I think I am pretty… I feel kind of really hot all the time… I haven’t actually done any temperature reading,” indicating feeling hot/febrile without measured temperature.

Patient says, “I’m trying to drink a lot of water,” and later, “it just feels like the fluids do go down, but it just feels like it’s going straight through… just come out pretty loose,” indicating ongoing diarrhea despite fluid intake.
Patient reports, “I had some lunch today, but again, it just come out pretty loose,” confirming ability to eat lunch with continued loose stools.

On urination: Doctor asks, “Are you passing urine? Okay.” Patient replies, “Yeah, but I guess less frequently maybe, but it seems to be okay,” consistent with urine not clearly abnormal but somewhat reduced/variable.
Doctor asks about blood in stools; patient responds, “No, I don’t remember anything… I think it’s just nothing like that. There’s nothing like that,” confirming no blood in stool.

Patient says, “my brother has had… something like this… He has it as well, for five days,” and “I’m not… I can’t think of what the trigger is for me,” which supports similar symptoms in brother and no clear dietary trigger identified.
When asked about medical history, patient says, “Yeah, I think otherwise I’m fit. Well… I can’t think of any related medical history… no, I don’t think so,” indicating generally healthy.
No mention is made of any prior surgeries in the transcript, so stating a lack of surgical history introduces new information not discussed.
Regarding medications, patient says, “I’ve been taking some, like, paracetamols and stuff like that lately, but… I’m not on any regular medication,” consistent with as‑needed paracetamol use.

Doctor advises, “you can get things like diurelite, which is a fluid replacement we can get from the pharmacy… No, you can just get over the counter,” matching recommendation for an oral rehydration solution such as Dioralyte OTC.

Doctor says, “You can try just, you know, regular paracetamol if you are feeling feverish,” and later, “If you’ve got bit of tummy pain, if you’re feeling feverish, then I think paracetamol is very sensible,” recommending paracetamol as needed for fever or pain.
On allergies, patient states, “I don’t have any allergies that I know of,” consistent with no known drug allergies.
Patient reports, “My dad actually has colon cancer at the moment… he’s sort of in his third stage,” supporting colon cancer in father currently in third stage.
Patient says, “I smoke… socially but not like regularly… normally if it’s a Friday… I might have a cigarette,” confirming social smoking.

On alcohol use, patient says, “I might have a beer during the weekdays… on Fridays I have more alcohol… not every week but maybe once or twice a month… we’ll drink a lot,” consistent with occasional alcohol drinking.
Patient states, “I work at an office in central London… I work in government,” matching work in a government office in central London.
On home situation, patient says, “I live with my um, sister and my mum,” supporting that he lives with his mother and sister.
Patient notes, “my brother has had, actually had something like this… He has it as well, for five days as well,” showing that his brother has also been ill recently.

Doctor’s assessment: “your symptoms are suggestive of something called gastroenteritis… you are losing a lot of fluid there… if you are getting dehydrated, then we need to do further investigations,” alongside diarrhea and crampy abdominal pain described earlier, supports diagnosis of acute gastroenteritis with diarrhea predominance and risk of dehydration.

Family history: “My dad actually has colon cancer at the moment… he’s sort of in his third stage,” which is an advanced stage; doctor says, “I’ll make a note of that because it’s always important,” supporting that family history is notable for advanced colon cancer in father.

Doctor advises, “you can get things like diurelite, which is a fluid replacement… from the pharmacy… No, you can just get over the counter,” matching plan to use OTC oral rehydration solution such as Dioralyte.
Doctor instructs, “clear fluids… soft diet, things like soup, mash, and then gradually build up as much as your body can tolerate,” aligning with clear fluids and soft diet advancing as tolerated.

Doctor says, “You can try just… regular paracetamol if you are feeling feverish,” and later, “If you’ve got bit of tummy pain, if you’re feeling feverish, then I think paracetamol is very sensible,” which is paracetamol as needed for fever and pain.
Doctor advises explicitly, “Try and avoid alcohol if you can,” matching recommendation to avoid alcohol.

There is no mention of prescribing antibiotics; management discussed is fluids, oral rehydration solution, paracetamol, and diet. Thus, “No antibiotics are prescribed… supportive care is to be continued” accurately reflects the transcript.
Doctor states, “if your symptoms aren’t settling down in the next couple of days, so 48 hours, I want you to give me a call back,” which matches follow‑up if no improvement in 48 hours.
